medical.title: Arsenic drug combo resurrects 'guardian of the genome' to fight aggressive blood cancers
medical.summary: A combination cancer therapy that relies on the reactivation of a tumor suppressor protein to kill leukemic and other blood cancer cells has shown promise in a small pilot trial.

medical.title: How the tumor environment influences bowel cancer cells' behavior and chemotherapy response
medical.summary: New research led by experts at the University of Nottingham has revealed how collagen in the tumor environment can alter bowel cancer cell behavior and influence inflammatory responses to chemotherapy, highlighting potential new avenues for future research into cancer treatment. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research, highlight the importance of the environment surrounding cancer cells in shaping how they behave and respond to treatment.

medical.title: Cell-level analysis reveals how ovarian tumors may develop resistance to chemotherapy
medical.summary: High-grade serous ovarian cancer is an aggressive form of ovarian cancer, characterized in particular by high diversity among the cells that compose a given tumor. This intratumor heterogeneity is a major challenge in understanding why some tumors respond to treatments and others resist. Additionally, this diversity is not limited to genetic differences: tumor cells that have similar genetic profiles may have different functions, depending on the genes they express and their epigenetic state.

medical.title: Japan's telemedicine use increased from 2020 to 2024 as age gap widened
medical.summary: Telemedicine came into wide use during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. However, access to and use of telemedicine may vary according to factors such as age, educational attainment, income, employment status and place of residence, though it has long been unclear whether these disparities would narrow as the use of telemedicine spread.

medical.title: Researchers develop privacy-friendly, secure and sustainable AI techniques for medical imaging
medical.summary: Artificial intelligence can be helpful in analyzing medical images and support radiotherapy planning workflows. However, huge amounts of sensitive patient data are needed to train robust AI models. Researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) have investigated how hospitals can jointly develop AI models for radiation therapy applications without exchanging such data. In their project, they use federated learning, a process in which a single model is trained at a decentralized location while the data remains in place. Their results demonstrate not only the technical feasibility of the approach but also its safe, more sustainable, and accessible use.

medical.title: Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age
medical.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden defense mechanism in aging muscles that sacrifices strength to protect cells from damage. In mice, partially restoring a crucial molecule reversed signs of muscle wasting and prevented premature death, raising hopes for new treatments for age-related muscle decline.

medical.title: Running distance is associated with how female runners distribute their daily energy expenditure
medical.summary: Generally, total energy expenditure is expected to be higher in individuals with greater physical activity. However, the constrained total energy expenditure model suggests that greater energy expenditure during exercise may be offset by lower energy expenditure during other activities or physiological processes, thereby maintaining total energy expenditure within a relatively limited range. It is unclear whether similar patterns occur in athletes engaged in long-term endurance training.

medical.title: Animal and plant proteins show different associations with testosterone levels in men
medical.summary: Higher animal protein intake was associated with lower blood testosterone levels, while higher plant protein intake was associated with higher levels, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland. The findings were published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition.

medical.title: Preclinical research shows macrophages can be programmed to fight solid cancer tumors
medical.summary: One person dies every 50 seconds in the U.S. from cancer, and an estimated 39% of people in the country will develop cancer during their lifetime. Survival rates have improved in recent decades from innovations and combinations of treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy and biotechnology. Still, some cancers resist treatment or recur.

medical.title: Don't let Halloween scare your heart health
medical.summary: Halloween season is a time for scary tricks and sweet treats. But people with heart conditions may need to take extra precautions before participating in fright nights. Baylor College of Medicine cardiologist and electrophysiologist Dr. Mohamed Gabr explains what you need to know to keep your heart healthy during this spooky season.

medical.title: Fighting cancer also means fighting against social stigma
medical.summary: Cancer-related discrimination arises from long-lasting cultural and institutional misconceptions, with significant impacts on every part of a person's quality of life and health—and Flinders University researchers say it requires coordinated policy, legal, institutional and public education responses for change to occur.

medical.title: Improve IBD bowel checks for early cancer detection
medical.summary: The first U.K.-wide analysis of bowel screening for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has identified opportunities to improve the early detection of cancer. The study—the largest of its kind globally—found that checks performed by professionals with regular experience, more time allowed for the procedure and the use of a special dye to improve visibility were each associated with finding small growths called polyps, which may become cancer.

medical.title: LSD and psilocybin push brain blood flow in opposite directions, study suggests
medical.summary: Psychedelics are a class of compounds that alter people's perceptions, mood and mental processes. Recent clinical studies suggest that some of these compounds, such as lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and psilocybin, could be promising for the treatment of depression and other psychiatric disorders.

medical.title: Promising AI-based approach to early detection of suicide-related behavior at emergency rooms
medical.summary: Researchers from the University of Johannesburg (UJ) have published a promising approach to identifying people at risk of suicide-related behavior (SRB) in the journal Scientific Reports.

medical.title: NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon
medical.summary: NASA’s Artemis I mission has revealed that cosmic radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but not by as much as scientists might expect. Tiny experimental detectors also uncovered surprising details about how radiation passes through the human body, offering valuable insights for future lunar exploration.

medical.title: Positive News launches new video podcast exploring what’s going right in the world
medical.summary: The What Went Right series is expanding to YouTube and other podcast platforms, bringing its weekly roundup of progress to new audiences The post Positive News launches new video podcast exploring what’s going right in the world appeared first on Positive News .

science.title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
science.summary: A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad.

science.title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
science.summary: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

science.title: Nature-inspired additive could help protect living cells during freezing and thawing
science.summary: In Australia, around 2,000 people are on the waiting list to receive an organ transplant, but thanks to new research being undertaken at the University of New England (UNE), this number could someday be significantly reduced.

science.title: A 60-year search is over: Chemists isolate long-elusive molecules with boron-oxygen triple bonds
science.summary: In a new publication in the journal Nature Chemistry, chemists in professor Holger Braunschweig's team at the University of Würzburg, supported by computational work from the team of professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India, detail their discovery of a method for preparing and isolating a range of surprisingly stable oxoboranes—a challenge that has stood for over 60 years.

science.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky—this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
science.summary: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects? It's earwax.

science.title: Amber fossils reveal how ancient Australian landmass helped seed Southeast Asia's tropical forests
science.summary: A landmass that broke away from northwestern Australia about 150 million years ago and drifted north for the next 100 million years helped lay the foundations for Southeast Asia's extraordinarily diverse tropical forests, new research has revealed.

science.title: Ants prioritize brain energy during starvation, echoing pattern seen in humans
science.summary: The human brain accounts for roughly 2% of total body weight but uses approximately 20% of our body's energy. Relative to our body size, human brains are much larger than those of other mammals and take a lot of energy to keep humans going. The evolution of our unusually large "social brain" is thought to have given us advanced intelligence and enabled the formation of large, complex societies.

science.title: Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders
science.summary: Researchers have discovered a surprising hidden ability in Europe's familiar black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light. The mysterious fluorescence comes mainly from glands in their skin and their toxic secretions, which can continue glowing for more than 24 hours after being released.

science.title: Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
science.summary: Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.

science.title: Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
science.summary: When two objects touch and then separate, they can swap tiny amounts of electric charge, even if they are made from exactly the same material. This 'triboelectric effect' is the source of everyday static electricity, but it is still poorly understood in large samples of powder, where vast numbers of particles are constantly colliding with each other.

science.title: Study finds heat waves speed snowmelt substantially, but rivers respond unevenly
science.summary: A new study by researchers at Montana State University has found that heat waves substantially accelerate the melting rate of mountain snowpack; however, the resulting water doesn't necessarily produce an immediate increase in streamflow.

science.title: Fishmeal alternative aims to protect marine wildlife from overfishing
science.summary: Technology that transforms organic waste into animal feed could help ease an overreliance on fishmeal in aquaculture. University of Queensland researchers have developed a production process that converts organic waste into biogas to grow a high-protein alternative to fish feed.

science.title: Machine learning simulations reveal how plastic transforms into hard carbon
science.summary: In a new study published in Chemical Science, researchers from the University of Oxford's Department of Chemistry have used machine learning simulations to trace how a common polymer transforms into hard carbon, revealing the atomic-scale processes that give this technologically important material its disordered structure.

science.title: Why do people self-harm? The mind-body divide might hold some clues
science.summary: In Finnish lore, the goddess Kivutar stashes away pain in a mountain for safekeeping. And yet she's also a healer, channeling it into rocks or boiling it down into a less potent form in a huge vat.

science.title: U.S. moves to weaken methane limits on oil and gas producers
science.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump announced Tuesday a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas superpollutant.

science.title: Comets probably didn't seed life on Earth after all, new study suggests
science.summary: The theory that comets delivered the molecular building blocks for life on Earth is a long-standing one, since comets are known to carry many of these molecules. However, a new study challenges this idea.

science.title: Major Southern Hemisphere ocean layer shifts, raising questions about heat and carbon storage
science.summary: The Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW)—a vast layer of fresh water spanning much of the Southern Hemisphere's ocean—has rapidly reversed its long-term trends in salinity and density, according to new research. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen and drive global ocean currents.

science.title: DNA analysis identifies root-dwelling fungi as potential keystone species in forest microbial communities
science.summary: Beneath the forest floor extends a vast ecosystem where a diverse array of microorganisms inhabit soil and root systems. Here, fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in processes such as nutrient cycling and carbon sequestration. Within these microbial communities may exist a keystone species, which exerts a disproportionately large influence on the entire structure and function of such an ecosystem.

environment.title: Persian leopards hang on in the Caucasus despite landmines
environment.summary: There have been few sightings of the endangered Persian leopard in the Caucasus region over the past 20 years: just three in Georgia and 10 in Armenia. But scientists and conservationists are alert to one Persian leopard in particular, whom they’ve named Aren and who is presumed to have journeyed 240 kilometers (150 miles) through […]

environment.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.

environment.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
environment.summary: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells.

environment.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
environment.summary: Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory.

environment.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
environment.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

environment.title: NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth
environment.summary: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moon’s bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions.

environment.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
environment.summary: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.

environment.title: Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
environment.summary: Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons. NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser-ranging satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.

mix_items.title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
mix_items.summary: A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad.

mix_items.summary: Peste 500 de copii au participat la activități de educație nonformală și wellbeing derulate de Fundația Inocenți cu sprijinul Pepco România. The post Sute de copii sprijiniți prin educație nonformală de Inocenți și Pepco appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.summary: A combination cancer therapy that relies on the reactivation of a tumor suppressor protein to kill leukemic and other blood cancer cells has shown promise in a small pilot trial.

mix_items.title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Nature-inspired additive could help protect living cells during freezing and thawing
mix_items.summary: In Australia, around 2,000 people are on the waiting list to receive an organ transplant, but thanks to new research being undertaken at the University of New England (UNE), this number could someday be significantly reduced.

mix_items.title: How the tumor environment influences bowel cancer cells' behavior and chemotherapy response
mix_items.summary: New research led by experts at the University of Nottingham has revealed how collagen in the tumor environment can alter bowel cancer cell behavior and influence inflammatory responses to chemotherapy, highlighting potential new avenues for future research into cancer treatment. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental & Clinical Cancer Research, highlight the importance of the environment surrounding cancer cells in shaping how they behave and respond to treatment.

mix_items.title: Cell-level analysis reveals how ovarian tumors may develop resistance to chemotherapy
mix_items.summary: High-grade serous ovarian cancer is an aggressive form of ovarian cancer, characterized in particular by high diversity among the cells that compose a given tumor. This intratumor heterogeneity is a major challenge in understanding why some tumors respond to treatments and others resist. Additionally, this diversity is not limited to genetic differences: tumor cells that have similar genetic profiles may have different functions, depending on the genes they express and their epigenetic state.

mix_items.title: A 60-year search is over: Chemists isolate long-elusive molecules with boron-oxygen triple bonds
mix_items.summary: In a new publication in the journal Nature Chemistry, chemists in professor Holger Braunschweig's team at the University of Würzburg, supported by computational work from the team of professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India, detail their discovery of a method for preparing and isolating a range of surprisingly stable oxoboranes—a challenge that has stood for over 60 years.

mix_items.title: Earwax is both slippery and sticky—this weird combo might lead to safer insect repellents
mix_items.summary: What has the consistency of both toothpaste and dough, can absorb twice its weight in water and still remain sticky, was used by medieval artists as a binder in paint and has been hypothesized by physicians to repel insects? It's earwax.

mix_items.title: Amber fossils reveal how ancient Australian landmass helped seed Southeast Asia's tropical forests
mix_items.summary: A landmass that broke away from northwestern Australia about 150 million years ago and drifted north for the next 100 million years helped lay the foundations for Southeast Asia's extraordinarily diverse tropical forests, new research has revealed.

mix_items.title: Japan's telemedicine use increased from 2020 to 2024 as age gap widened
mix_items.summary: Telemedicine came into wide use during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. However, access to and use of telemedicine may vary according to factors such as age, educational attainment, income, employment status and place of residence, though it has long been unclear whether these disparities would narrow as the use of telemedicine spread.

mix_items.title: Researchers develop privacy-friendly, secure and sustainable AI techniques for medical imaging
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence can be helpful in analyzing medical images and support radiotherapy planning workflows. However, huge amounts of sensitive patient data are needed to train robust AI models. Researchers at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) have investigated how hospitals can jointly develop AI models for radiation therapy applications without exchanging such data. In their project, they use federated learning, a process in which a single model is trained at a decentralized location while the data remains in place. Their results demonstrate not only the technical feasibility of the approach but also its safe, more sustainable, and accessible use.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden defense mechanism in aging muscles that sacrifices strength to protect cells from damage. In mice, partially restoring a crucial molecule reversed signs of muscle wasting and prevented premature death, raising hopes for new treatments for age-related muscle decline.

mix_items.title: Ants prioritize brain energy during starvation, echoing pattern seen in humans
mix_items.summary: The human brain accounts for roughly 2% of total body weight but uses approximately 20% of our body's energy. Relative to our body size, human brains are much larger than those of other mammals and take a lot of energy to keep humans going. The evolution of our unusually large "social brain" is thought to have given us advanced intelligence and enabled the formation of large, complex societies.

mix_items.title: Running distance is associated with how female runners distribute their daily energy expenditure
mix_items.summary: Generally, total energy expenditure is expected to be higher in individuals with greater physical activity. However, the constrained total energy expenditure model suggests that greater energy expenditure during exercise may be offset by lower energy expenditure during other activities or physiological processes, thereby maintaining total energy expenditure within a relatively limited range. It is unclear whether similar patterns occur in athletes engaged in long-term endurance training.

mix_items.title: Animal and plant proteins show different associations with testosterone levels in men
mix_items.summary: Higher animal protein intake was associated with lower blood testosterone levels, while higher plant protein intake was associated with higher levels, according to a new study from the University of Eastern Finland. The findings were published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition.

mix_items.title: Preclinical research shows macrophages can be programmed to fight solid cancer tumors
mix_items.summary: One person dies every 50 seconds in the U.S. from cancer, and an estimated 39% of people in the country will develop cancer during their lifetime. Survival rates have improved in recent decades from innovations and combinations of treatments, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, immunotherapy and biotechnology. Still, some cancers resist treatment or recur.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a secret glow in toxic fire salamanders
mix_items.summary: Researchers have discovered a surprising hidden ability in Europe's familiar black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light. The mysterious fluorescence comes mainly from glands in their skin and their toxic secretions, which can continue glowing for more than 24 hours after being released.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.

mix_items.title: Don't let Halloween scare your heart health
mix_items.summary: Halloween season is a time for scary tricks and sweet treats. But people with heart conditions may need to take extra precautions before participating in fright nights. Baylor College of Medicine cardiologist and electrophysiologist Dr. Mohamed Gabr explains what you need to know to keep your heart healthy during this spooky season.

mix_items.title: Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
mix_items.summary: When two objects touch and then separate, they can swap tiny amounts of electric charge, even if they are made from exactly the same material. This 'triboelectric effect' is the source of everyday static electricity, but it is still poorly understood in large samples of powder, where vast numbers of particles are constantly colliding with each other.

mix_items.title: Study finds heat waves speed snowmelt substantially, but rivers respond unevenly
mix_items.summary: A new study by researchers at Montana State University has found that heat waves substantially accelerate the melting rate of mountain snowpack; however, the resulting water doesn't necessarily produce an immediate increase in streamflow.

mix_items.title: Fighting cancer also means fighting against social stigma
mix_items.summary: Cancer-related discrimination arises from long-lasting cultural and institutional misconceptions, with significant impacts on every part of a person's quality of life and health—and Flinders University researchers say it requires coordinated policy, legal, institutional and public education responses for change to occur.

mix_items.title: Fishmeal alternative aims to protect marine wildlife from overfishing
mix_items.summary: Technology that transforms organic waste into animal feed could help ease an overreliance on fishmeal in aquaculture. University of Queensland researchers have developed a production process that converts organic waste into biogas to grow a high-protein alternative to fish feed.

mix_items.title: Improve IBD bowel checks for early cancer detection
mix_items.summary: The first U.K.-wide analysis of bowel screening for patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) has identified opportunities to improve the early detection of cancer. The study—the largest of its kind globally—found that checks performed by professionals with regular experience, more time allowed for the procedure and the use of a special dye to improve visibility were each associated with finding small growths called polyps, which may become cancer.

mix_items.title: LSD and psilocybin push brain blood flow in opposite directions, study suggests
mix_items.summary: Psychedelics are a class of compounds that alter people's perceptions, mood and mental processes. Recent clinical studies suggest that some of these compounds, such as lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and psilocybin, could be promising for the treatment of depression and other psychiatric disorders.

mix_items.title: Machine learning simulations reveal how plastic transforms into hard carbon
mix_items.summary: In a new study published in Chemical Science, researchers from the University of Oxford's Department of Chemistry have used machine learning simulations to trace how a common polymer transforms into hard carbon, revealing the atomic-scale processes that give this technologically important material its disordered structure.

mix_items.title: Why do people self-harm? The mind-body divide might hold some clues
mix_items.summary: In Finnish lore, the goddess Kivutar stashes away pain in a mountain for safekeeping. And yet she's also a healer, channeling it into rocks or boiling it down into a less potent form in a huge vat.

mix_items.title: Promising AI-based approach to early detection of suicide-related behavior at emergency rooms
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of Johannesburg (UJ) have published a promising approach to identifying people at risk of suicide-related behavior (SRB) in the journal Scientific Reports.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Artemis I mission has revealed that cosmic radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but not by as much as scientists might expect. Tiny experimental detectors also uncovered surprising details about how radiation passes through the human body, offering valuable insights for future lunar exploration.

mix_items.title: U.S. moves to weaken methane limits on oil and gas producers
mix_items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump announced Tuesday a sweeping rollback of rules that stop oil and gas producers from emitting methane, a greenhouse gas superpollutant.

mix_items.title: Comets probably didn't seed life on Earth after all, new study suggests
mix_items.summary: The theory that comets delivered the molecular building blocks for life on Earth is a long-standing one, since comets are known to carry many of these molecules. However, a new study challenges this idea.

mix_items.title: Major Southern Hemisphere ocean layer shifts, raising questions about heat and carbon storage
mix_items.summary: The Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW)—a vast layer of fresh water spanning much of the Southern Hemisphere's ocean—has rapidly reversed its long-term trends in salinity and density, according to new research. The AAIW helps store carbon, supply oxygen and drive global ocean currents.

mix_items.title: Positive News launches new video podcast exploring what’s going right in the world
mix_items.summary: The What Went Right series is expanding to YouTube and other podcast platforms, bringing its weekly roundup of progress to new audiences The post Positive News launches new video podcast exploring what’s going right in the world appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: DNA analysis identifies root-dwelling fungi as potential keystone species in forest microbial communities
mix_items.summary: Beneath the forest floor extends a vast ecosystem where a diverse array of microorganisms inhabit soil and root systems. Here, fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in processes such as nutrient cycling and carbon sequestration. Within these microbial communities may exist a keystone species, which exerts a disproportionately large influence on the entire structure and function of such an ecosystem.

mix_items.title: Persian leopards hang on in the Caucasus despite landmines
mix_items.summary: There have been few sightings of the endangered Persian leopard in the Caucasus region over the past 20 years: just three in Georgia and 10 in Armenia. But scientists and conservationists are alert to one Persian leopard in particular, whom they’ve named Aren and who is presumed to have journeyed 240 kilometers (150 miles) through […]

mix_items.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.

mix_items.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
mix_items.summary: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells.

mix_items.title: NASA captures a stunning transformation in Australia's red outback
mix_items.summary: Australia's normally dry, rust-colored outback has erupted into a spectacular carpet of wildflowers after unusually heavy rains, potentially producing its most impressive bloom in nearly 20 years. NASA satellite images capture the stunning transformation, which has even brought rare flowers to the grounds of a remote deep-space observatory.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

mix_items.title: NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth
mix_items.summary: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moon’s bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions.

mix_items.title: Scientists changed how zoo lions eat. Their wild side came out
mix_items.summary: Giving zoo lions whole carcasses on a feast-and-fast schedule appears to bring out more natural behavior. The lions spent nearly three times longer feeding, engaged in more tearing and manipulating of food, and rested more heavily after meals. Their activity then increased gradually during the fasting period, closely resembling the rhythm seen in wild lions.

mix_items.title: Earth’s center is moving, and NASA just measured it
mix_items.summary: Earth’s center of mass is constantly on the move, shifting by a few millimeters as enormous amounts of water, ice, and even air migrate around the planet with the seasons. NASA scientists have developed a more precise way to track these tiny swings using laser-ranging satellites, GPS data, and measurements of how water and ice deform Earth’s crust.
